look_here_first: TEXAS WILD-RICE (*Zizania texana*) — ENDANGERED. See long submerged ribbonlike leaves streaming in upper San Marcos River; actual USFWS river photographs cover this gross habit. At flowering, LOWER spreading branches bear pendent awnless staminate units/anthers; UPPER more ascending branches produce slender awned pistillate spikelets. NEW USFWS gallery panels 9–10 now show flowering branch architecture and awned-looking green units, but do NOT prove exact individual female lemma awn or continuous same-panicle sex map. Both actual underwater ROOTED CROWN and 5–15mm true inner membranous LIGULE are STILL missing; acquire only authorized existing ex-situ conservation photographs, never manipulate wild endangered plants. Look-alikes Zizaniopsis miliacea and Leersia oryzoides now have clearly labeled source-licensed comparison photographs.
photo_note:
Eight physically archived species JPEGs now exist (three Joey Santore CC BY-NC; five Ryan Hagerty/USFWS public-domain). This is a source inventory, not proof of public rendering, image-level anatomical identity or 100% readiness. Original source JPEG reviewed 2026-10-21, 2 true visible-structure arrows. Species-complete macro work still open. 2026-10-24: All three original locally stored Joey images inspected. Six anatomy/habitat arrows added to the two unreviewed panels; original two retained. CC BY-NC is not a public publishing grant; retain need for separate author reuse permission documentation; seek USFWS PD replacements. Lane 4 four-role evidence audit 2026-10-26: original USFWS 20535/20580/20562 actual pixels inspected; no roots or true inner ligule exposed and no complete sex-separated panicle. Preserve 3 conditionally noncommercial iNaturalist photos and 5 PD FWS originals, no photo deletion or guessed labels.
2026-10-27 Lane4 protected Zizania: Three additional actual Ryan Hagerty USFWS public domain photos physically archived, confirmed original bytes/image rights, nine new arrows. 20578 particularly shows true connected flower axis with upper erect narrow female-zone units and lower spreading male branches carrying yellow anthers; 20576 close shows genuine male anthers; 20561 stream-swept ribbon foliage. No root or true ligule, no individual female lemma tip measurement, no touching. New first formal photo role estimate 3.5/6 (58%), with safety status unchanged.

best_field_traits: TEXAS WILD-RICE (*Zizania texana*) is a federally/state ENDANGERED aquatic perennial endemic to the upper San Marcos River in Hays County. Long ribbonlike underwater leaves align with current; flowering shoots can emerge. Species bears separate male and female flowers arranged on branching flowerhead sections. This source photo shows yellow anthers on a flowering spray. Observe only—NEVER pull, harvest, transplant, or trample; photograph from permitted positions.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: No-contact whole flowing-water habit photograph showing submerged long leaves
Male flowers with yellow anthers and separate female floral units from permitted vantage
Leaf midrib and true ligule without handling plants
Compare species against co-occurring river grasses with nonintrusive photography
crew_field_check: Zizaniopsis miliacea/giant cutgrass grows in large emergent reedlike marsh clumps with a broad airy panicle; Leersia oryzoides has scratchy leaf edges and rice-like one-flowered spikelets, but is not equivalent to rare Texas wild-rice. Use precise live river habitat plus leaf/inflorescence anatomy and expert determination; no invasive management or routine native planting recommendations.
FEDERALLY + STATE ENDANGERED. Non-contact study only, protected Hays County endemic; no plant handling/collection/disturbance.

NO-CONTACT FLOWER KEY: male spikelets on LOWER panicle branches (7–9 mm, awnless, visible anthers), female on UPPER branches (~10 mm with one ~10–20 mm lemma awn). Ordinary glumes absent/obscure; published ranges, not current gallery measurements.
Giant cutgrass differs in male/female placement along the SAME flowering branch; Texas wild-rice separates male lower and female upper BRANCHES. Never enter or manipulate endangered stands to verify.
PHOTO GAP: true ligule and female awn not resolved by present verified annotations; preserve existing two gross-feature arrows only.

measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.growth_form: Submerged aquatic perennial, with rooted stolons and ribbonlike underwater leaves; USFWS describes clonal growth. GrassBase's morphology paragraph labels the plant annual even though its Kew overview and USFWS call it perennial; preserve that source conflict rather than changing canonical biology.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.ligule_collar: Published GrassBase: eciliate MEMBRANOUS ligule 5–15 mm; blades 10–40 mm wide. These dimensions are source measurements, not demonstrated in the three stored photos. Do not manipulate endangered plants to expose a collar.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.flowering_architecture: Open panicle about 20–30 cm long; lower spreading branches with staminate (male) spikelets and upper ascending branches with pistillate (female) spikelets. Confirm branch origin in an intact image before placing sex-specific arrows.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.male_spikelet: Male spikelets linear 7–9 mm, awnless; male lemma five-veined. Yellow dangling anthers are male flower parts, not glumes or female awns.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.female_spikelet: Female spikelets narrow, about 10 mm and one-flowered; female lemma about 10 mm, three-veined, bearing one 10–20 mm awn (GrassBase). The 1986 species study reports 10–25 mm female awns; preserve range difference.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.glumes: Ordinary paired glumes ABSENT or obscure in both sexes; do not arrow nonexistent glumes or mistake lemma/palea for glumes.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.awn: The female lemma bears a single terminal awn, whereas male spikelets lack awns. Distinguish this structure from exposed anthers.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.local_lookalikes: Zizaniopsis miliacea (giant cutgrass): large emergent marsh grass, male and female spikelets on different positions along the SAME panicle branch, versus Zizania's lower male and upper female BRANCHES. Leersia oryzoides (rice cutgrass): rough-bladed wetland grass with flattened one-flowered spikelets, but not the same sex-separated flowering arrangement. Habitat or ribbonlike leaves alone cannot certify Z. texana.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Texas wild-rice — true female TOP vs male LOWER floral branching, entirely no-contact
steps: FIRST observe from a permitted, non-intrusive place without touching or entering a protected stand. New public-domain USFWS panel 11 (index10) shows genuinely long submerged ribbon blades streaming with current and one upright flowering stem. Neither the current nor visible sediment proves an exposed attached root.

MOST IMPORTANT photo panel 13 (index12): the continuous upright inflorescence axis shows ascending narrow TOP flowering branches (the female region described by Texas Parks and Wildlife) and open, outward-spreading LOWER branches with visible dangling yellow male anthers. No collection or branch bending is necessary. Position of each branch is more diagnostic than the distant water texture.

Panel 12 (index11): close-up of male staminate flowers, pale elongated parts and visible yellow dangling anthers. These are ANTHERS, not a female awn or seeds. The photographer's picture is research imagery; crew should not recreate it by handling plants.

USFWS existing panels 9–10 (indices8–9) show broad flowering architecture and slender awned-looking organs, but the photo alone cannot isolate the exact female lemma-to-single-awns attachment. No ruler is visible.

Protected species has described smooth 5–15mm INTERNAL membranous ligule. None of the 13 real source photos exposes this internal free tongue with a ruler, so no image earns a collar/ligule role. Use separately approved ex-situ greenhouse propagation specimen photography only if institutional authorization and rights allow it.
Actual submerged same-plant rooted crown or stolon-node attachment remains unphotographed. Do not infer from adjacent sediment or stones and NEVER dig or pull wild Texas wild-rice for training.

Other-species comparisons now in panels14–15 (indices13–14): giant cutgrass *Zizaniopsis miliacea* and rice cutgrass *Leersia oryzoides*. These are NOT Texas wild-rice and do not supply its glume and awn micrographs.

Existing Joey Santore source photographs (indices0–2) are CC BY-NC with appropriate photographer/source terms, not federal public domain. All added source USFWS photos are independently public domain.

Score only observed structures: submerged flowering growth/habit 1, no true roots 0, no inner ligule 0, complete sex-region flowering axis 1, visible reproductive anther/awn-like macro 0.5 (no demonstrated female lemma tip), independent labeled comparable other-taxon photos 1. Total 3.5/6=58%, not public-fully-ready.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Identify endangered Texas wild-rice from legally permitted observation only: ribbon leaves streaming in running water, emerge a flowering axis, follow top ascending female-bearing and lower spreading male-bearing floral regions with dangling anthers. Final uncertain identifications belong to authorized botanical specialists. Do not touch/enter/collect protected plants.
